steps.markdown:
To write the equation of a line that passes through a point $P$ (with position vector $\mathbf{p}$) and has a direction vector $\mathbf{v},$ one option is to use the vector equation of the line:

$$
\begin{aligned}r &=p+tv,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

However, there is also another way, which is to write the **equation of a line using the cross product**, as follows:

$$
(\mathbf{r}-  \mathbf{p} ) \times \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}
$$

For example, suppose that we have a line that passes through the point $P(4,1,-5)$ and has a direction vector $\mathbf{v}=\langle 1,0,-1 \rangle$ (see the picture below).

![](images/6c/6cd052e948a46524e08b1305a59019b052e71c7b9ce6e5376f49c4cbcc56a737.png)

The equation of the line can be written as follows:

$$
(\mathbf{r}-\langle 4,1,-5 \rangle) \times \langle 1,0,-1 \rangle = \mathbf{0}
$$

To understand why the formula works, notice that for any point $R,$ this point lies on the line if and only if the vector $\overrightarrow{PR}$ is parallel to $\mathbf{v}.$ Now, we know that the cross product of two parallel vectors is always $\mathbf{0}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\overrightarrow{PR} \parallel \mathbf{v} 
	\quad\Leftrightarrow\quad 
	\overrightarrow{PR} \times \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}
$$

So, since $\overrightarrow{PR} = \mathbf{r}-\mathbf{p},$ we get the desired equation

$$
(\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{p}) \times \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}.
$$

\frac{x-(-8)}{2}=\frac{y-2}{10}=\frac{z-(-9)}{-8}

steps.markdown:
The vector equation of a line is given by 

$$
(r-\begin{bmatrix}5 \\ 3 \\ 6\end{bmatrix})\times \begin{bmatrix}-9 \\ -8 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}=0.
$$

Find its parametric equations.
steps.solution:
The equation of the line using the cross product takes the general form

$$
(r-p)\times v=0.
$$

Comparing this general form to the given equation, we find that

- the vector $v=\begin{bmatrix}-9 \\ -8 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}$ is parallel to the line, and

- $p=\begin{bmatrix}5 \\ 3 \\ 6\end{bmatrix}$ is the position vector of the point $P(5,3,6)$ that lies on the line.

Therefore, the given vector equation can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =\begin{bmatrix}5 \\ 3 \\ 6\end{bmatrix}+t\begin{bmatrix}-9 \\ -8 \\ 2\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}5 \\ 3 \\ 6\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}-9t \\ -8t \\ 2t\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}5-9t \\ 3-8t \\ 6+2t\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

and finally, the parametric equations are

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=5-9t \\ y &=3-8t \\ z &=6+2t\end{aligned}\right.
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$
steps.title: Converting Between Parametric and Cross Product Form for a Given Straight Line

steps.markdown:
If we have an equation of a line in the form $\left( \mathbf{r} - \mathbf{p} \right) \times \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0},$ we can expand the parentheses, though we must remember that the cross product is non-commutative. This gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}(r-p)\times v & =0 \\ r\times v-p\times v & =0 \\ r\times v & =p\times v.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $\mathbf{p}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ are both constant vectors, we can denote $\mathbf{c} = \mathbf{p} \times \mathbf{v}$ to simplify the equation. So, we obtain an alternative form of the equation of the line using the cross product:

$$
\mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{c}
$$

knowledgePoint.title: Finding the Cross Product Equation of a Line That Passes Through Two Points

steps.markdown: A line passes through the points $P(4,-7,9)$ and $Q(3,-5,8).$ Find its vector equation in the form $\mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{c}.$
steps.solution:
We know that the line passes through the points $P(4,-7,9)$ and $Q(3,-5,8)$. Now, we need to find a vector parallel to the given line. We can use the vector $\overrightarrow{PQ}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\overset{\to }{PQ} \\  & =q-p \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ -5 \\ 8\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ -7 \\ 9\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 2 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, starting with the equation of the line using the cross product, we manipulate the equation and then substitute in our values of $\mathbf{p}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(r-p)\times v & =0 \\ r\times v-p\times v & =0 \\ r\times v & =p\times v \\ r\times \begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 2 \\ -1\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ -7 \\ 9\end{bmatrix}\times \begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 2 \\ -1\end{bmatrix} \\ r\times \begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 2 \\ -1\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 4 & -7 & 9 \\ -1 & 2 & -1\end{vmatrix} \\ r\times \begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 2 \\ -1\end{bmatrix} & =-11i-5j+k\end{aligned}
$$

steps.markdown: A line passes through the points $P(-1,0,-5)$ and $Q(3,9,8).$ Find its vector equation in the form $(r-p)\times v=0.$
steps.solution:
We know that the line passes through the points $P(-1,0,-5)$ and $Q(3,9,8).$ Now, we need to find a vector parallel to the given line. We can use the vector $\overset{\to }{PQ}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\overset{\to }{PQ} \\  & =q-p \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 9 \\ 8\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 0 \\ -5\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 9 \\ 13\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to get the equation of the line using the cross product, we substitute in our values of $p$ and $v$ as follows:

$$
(r-\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 0 \\ -5\end{bmatrix})\times \begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 9 \\ 13\end{bmatrix}=0.
$$

steps.markdown: A line passes through the points  $P(6,3,1)$ and $Q(2,4,9).$ Find its vector equation in the form $r\times v=c.$
steps.solution:
We know that the line passes through the points $P(6,3,1)$ and $Q(2,4,9).$ Now, we need to find a vector parallel to the given line. We can use the vector $\overset{\to }{PQ}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\overset{\to }{PQ} \\  & =q-p \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 4 \\ 9\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}6 \\ 3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-4 \\ 1 \\ 8\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, starting with the equation of the line using the cross product, we manipulate the equation and then substitute in our values of $p$ and $v$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(r-p)\times v & =0 \\ r\times v-p\times v & =0 \\ r\times v & =p\times v \\ r\times \begin{bmatrix}-4 \\ 1 \\ 8\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}6 \\ 3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\times \begin{bmatrix}-4 \\ 1 \\ 8\end{bmatrix} \\ r\times \begin{bmatrix}-4 \\ 1 \\ 8\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 6 & 3 & 1 \\ -4 & 1 & 8\end{vmatrix} \\ r\times \begin{bmatrix}-4 \\ 1 \\ 8\end{bmatrix} & =23i-52j+18k.\end{aligned}
$$

steps.markdown: A line passes through the points $P(-2,2,6)$ and $Q(3,7,11).$ Find its vector equation in the form $r\times v=c.$
steps.solution:
We know that the line passes through the points $P(-2,2,6)$ and $Q(3,7,11).$ Now, we need to find a vector parallel to the given line. We can use the vector $\overset{\to }{PQ}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\overset{\to }{PQ} \\  & =q-p \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 7 \\ 11\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 2 \\ 6\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}5 \\ 5 \\ 5\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, starting with the equation of the line using the cross product, we manipulate the equation and then substitute in our values of $p$ and $v$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(r-p)\times v & =0 \\ r\times v-p\times v & =0 \\ r\times v & =p\times v \\ r\times \begin{bmatrix}5 \\ 5 \\ 5\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 2 \\ 6\end{bmatrix}\times \begin{bmatrix}5 \\ 5 \\ 5\end{bmatrix} \\ r\times \begin{bmatrix}5 \\ 5 \\ 5\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ -2 & 2 & 6 \\ 5 & 5 & 5\end{vmatrix} \\ r\times \begin{bmatrix}5 \\ 5 \\ 5\end{bmatrix} & =-20i+40j-20k.\end{aligned}
$$

steps.markdown: A line passes through the points  $P(-3,-1,4)$ and $Q(1,8,9).$ Find its vector equation in the form $r\times v=c.$
steps.solution:
Local correction by Codex. The five original Math Academy choices are retained; the additional correct equation is locally authored. Math Academy's grading key for the original bank is unconfirmed.

We need a vector parallel to the line. Using the two given points,

$$
v=q-p=\begin{bmatrix}1\\8\\9\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}-3\\-1\\4\end{bmatrix}
=\begin{bmatrix}4\\9\\5\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Starting with $(r-p)\times v=0$, we obtain $r\times v=p\times v$. Expanding the cross product gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
p\times v&=\begin{vmatrix}i&j&k\\-3&-1&4\\4&9&5\end{vmatrix}\\
&=(-5-36)i-(-15-16)j+(-27+4)k\\
&=-41i+31j-23k.
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus the equation is

$$
r\times\begin{bmatrix}4\\9\\5\end{bmatrix}=-41i+31j-23k.
$$

Both given points satisfy this equation: $P\times v=Q\times v=(-41,31,-23)$. None of the five original choices does.

Original Math Academy explanation (preserved verbatim below; its concluding signs are incorrect):

We know that the line passes through the points $P(-3,-1,4)$ and $Q(1,8,9).$ Now, we need to find a vector parallel to the given line. We can use the vector $\overset{\to }{PQ}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\overset{\to }{PQ} \\  & =q-p \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 8 \\ 9\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ -1 \\ 4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 9 \\ 5\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, starting with the equation of the line using the cross product, we manipulate the equation and then substitute in our values of $p$ and $v$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(r-p)\times v & =0 \\ r\times v-p\times v & =0 \\ r\times v & =p\times v \\ r\times \begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 9 \\ 5\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ -1 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}\times \begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 9 \\ 5\end{bmatrix} \\ r\times \begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 9 \\ 5\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ -3 & -1 & 4 \\ 4 & 9 & 5\end{vmatrix} \\ r\times \begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 9 \\ 5\end{bmatrix} & =-41i-31j+23k.\end{aligned}
$$
